summary: Suggests a mail protocol mapping between full RFC 822 messages and RFC 822 with restricted encoding, for the Internet and UK Academic communities. It asks for discussion and is not a standard. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1137 defines a way to encode difficult characters in RFC 822 email addresses for systems with a restricted character set. The receiver can decode the address back into its full form.

questions: mapping between rfc 822 and restricted encoding
how to encode rfc 822 addresses for uucp
what does #h# mean in an email address
how does restricted rfc 822 mapping work
subtitle: A reversible mapping for RFC 822 addresses crossing systems with restricted character sets.

tldr.problem: Some RFC 822 mail networks cannot carry every character allowed in a quoted local part, which can cause messages or replies to be lost.
tldr.mechanism: The mapping rewrites characters in the address local part using underscores and hash-delimited codes, then reverses the process at the other end.
tldr.outcome: The memo is Historic, updates RFC 976, and explicitly says it does not specify an Internet standard.

today: RFC 1137 is Historic and updates RFC 976. Its text says it does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Full and Restricted RFC 822
sections.content:
Full RFC 822 supports every legal address, including a quoted-string local part such as "Joe Soap"@foo.bar. Restricted RFC 822 is a subset that need not support quoted-string local parts; the RFC identifies standard UUCP mail transfer as an example.

When a full address crosses into a restricted system, information may be lost, including the ability to return an error. The memo describes a symmetric mapping to reduce this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail systems cannot carry every character in an address. This mapping changes those characters into a form that restricted systems can carry.

sections.title: Encoding and Decoding Characters
sections.content:
Characters allowed by the encoded atom pass through unchanged. A space becomes an underscore. Special codes include #u# for underscore, #l# and #r# for parentheses, and #h# for a hash. Other characters can use a three-digit decimal ASCII code between hash marks, from 0 to 127.

To encode, remove quoting from a quoted string, retain allowed characters, and encode the rest. To decode, reverse the mapping when the address parses as an encoded atom; otherwise, map its characters directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Allowed characters stay as they are. Spaces and other restricted characters get short codes that the receiving system can turn back into the original characters.

sections.title: Where the Mapping Applies
sections.content:
The mapping applies to the RFC 822 local part of addresses at the message-transfer or header level. The RFC shows a plain address that remains unchanged, a quoted name with a space that uses an underscore, and an address with a hash and tilde encoded using special and decimal forms.

The document asks for discussion and improvements and says it does not specify an Internet standard. Its metadata marks it Historic and records that it updates RFC 976.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the part before the at sign is transformed. Ordinary text can stay the same, while characters the restricted system cannot carry are encoded.

references.text: Horton, M., "UUCP Mail Interchange Format Standard", RFC 976, February 1986.
